what_its_for: Quinine is used to treat malaria, a serious infection caused by a parasite spread through mosquito bites. It is also sometimes used to relieve painful leg cramps, though this is not an FDA-approved use. Your doctor has prescribed this medicine for a specific reason — always use it only as directed.
how_to_take: Swallow the capsule whole with a full glass of water. You can take quinine with food or milk if it upsets your stomach. Do not crush, chew, or break open the capsules. Try to take it at the same times each day to keep a steady amount of the medicine in your body. Always complete the full course of treatment even if you start feeling better, unless your doctor tells you to stop.
dosing: For malaria in adults, the usual dose is 648 mg (two 324 mg capsules) taken by mouth three times a day for 3 to 7 days, depending on where the malaria was acquired. Your doctor may adjust your dose if you have kidney or liver problems. Always follow the exact dose and schedule your doctor prescribed — do not take more or less than directed.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one, as this can increase your risk of serious side effects.
storage: Store quinine capsules at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep the capsules away from light, heat, and moisture. Do not store them in the bathroom. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Do not use after the expiration date printed on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking antacids that contain aluminum or magnesium within 2 hours of taking quinine, as they can reduce how well the medicine works. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice, as they can increase quinine levels in your blood and raise the risk of side effects. Do not drink alcohol while taking this medicine. Avoid driving or using heavy machinery if quinine makes you feel dizzy or causes vision changes. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about ALL medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, as quinine can interact with many drugs including blood thinners, heart medicines, antifungals, and antibiotics.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: a fast, irregular, or pounding heartbeat; chest pain; severe dizziness or fainting; ringing in the ears (tinnitus) or hearing loss; blurred vision or vision changes; unusual bruising or bleeding; signs of low blood sugar such as sweating, shaking, or confusion; skin rash, itching, or hives; dark urine, yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice); or severe stomach pain. These could be signs of a serious or life-threatening reaction. Quinine can cause a dangerous heart rhythm problem, so tell your doctor immediately if you feel your heart beating abnormally.
when_it_works: You may start to feel better within a few days of starting quinine for malaria, but it is very important to finish your entire course of treatment. Stopping early can allow the infection to come back and may make it harder to treat. If your symptoms are not improving after a couple of days, or if they get worse, contact your doctor.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Quinine can harm an unborn baby. Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant or become pregnant while taking this medicine. However, untreated malaria in pregnancy can also be very dangerous, so your doctor will weigh the risks and benefits carefully. Breastfeeding: Small amounts of quinine pass into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding while on this medicine. Children: Safety and dosing in children under 16 years old should be determined by a doctor. Elderly: Older adults may be more sensitive to the effects of quinine, especially heart-related side effects. Kidney or liver problems: Your doctor may need to adjust your dose if your kidneys or liver are not working well.
